title: A gold mine has created a 'little town' in central Newfoundland — and it's about to get bigger
summary: Step inside the Valentine gold mine near Buchans, which is now Atlantic Canada's largest.

image.caption: Workers in the Valentine Gold pit near Buchans (Leigh Anne Power/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New
Step inside the Valentine gold mine near Buchans, which is now Atlantic Canada's largest.
The mine near Buchans is now the largest in Atlantic Canada
There's a new town in central Newfoundland and most people don't even know it exists.
It's not incorporated and doesn't have an official name, but its population is greater than that of all the closest communities combined.
This is the Valentine gold mine — the largest in Atlantic Canada — where thousands of people live and work.
"We're very much a little town here. Currently, we're about a thousand employees at the site at one time," said Jason Cyr, the VP of Canadian operations for mine owner Equinox Gold.

blocks.text: "So think about that, it's actually 2,000 because it's ... two weeks on and two weeks off."
The town with no name is driving a big part of the economy in the region, and it's going to get bigger.
Phase 2 construction starts in the new year, and it's expected to bring more long-term jobs in a region that's desperate for them.
The mine is undergoing a $436-million expansion and increasing gold production by about 25 per cent, Cyr said.
Jason Cyr is the manager of Canadian operations for Equinox Gold. (Leigh Anne Power/CBC)
It takes about three hours to reach the Valentine site once you turn off the Trans Canada Highway toward Buchans.
Most of that is over dirt roads, which become a river of mud when it rains and a whirlwind of dust when it doesn't. One section is so twisty, employees call it The Snake.
It's so tough to access, the company has supplied everything workers might need, from a gym to a recreation centre, to a cafeteria that provides 20 different sandwich options every day.
The site even has its own clinic, complete with paramedics and an ambulance.
At the rim of the Leprechaun pit, one of three the company works, giant dump trucks look like dinky cars, far far below. Gray rock covers the land like the surface of the moon.
'Liberate' the gold
This is where the gold journey begins, Cyr says.

"We drill and blast what you've seen out in the open pit. That gets trucked over to the crusher. We crush it from roughly 16 inches down to 4-6 inches in diameter. It goes into a storage stockpile, which then feeds a mill for further pulverization and liberation of the gold particle. Then it goes on to leaching, and then it's refined right here on site to a bar of 85-88 per cent purity," he explained.
From there, he says, Brinks picks up the refined gold and carries it out of the province where it's purified and then made into jewelry and coins.
The crusher at the Valentine gold mine pulverizes the raw ore. (Leigh Anne Power/CBC)
The whole vast operation is run from a control room, operated by Kyle Park.

"If this plant was a body, I'd be the brain," he said. "We control everything from this room, front to back, and try to recover as much gold as we can. Basically, we want to take the rock that comes in from the crusher and begin to turn it into a slurry so we can transport it throughout the system and recover as much as we can. Liberate some gold."
But not everybody is allowed to liberate the gold, Cyr says. Security is tight and background checks are completed, among other measures.
Workers coming home
Cyr says one of the things Equinox is most proud of is its commitment to local hiring. About 94 per cent of employees at the mine are from this province, including Shannon Parsons.

"This is my fifth mine now," he said. "I've worked all over Canada, in Ontario and Nunavut, but it's nice to be back home again. There's a lot of talent that worked out of province, same as myself. So people are looking for the opportunity to come home again."
And Cyr says the jobs people on site do are often very different from what outsiders might imagine.

"I like the vast skill set that mining brings. It's not just what you'd think growing up ... that there's pickaxes and such," he said. "It's the technology. It's the different skill sets from instrumentation to environment, health and safety, accounting, HR, mining, milling, electrical, mechanical. There's a lot of talent all on one site."
The company offers specific training on its equipment for those who are newer to mining. Mike Hann runs a state-of-the-art equipment simulator.

"We're set up to actually allow people to get control familiarization before they actually hit the field," he said. "So anybody who don't have prior experience, they can get used to the controls, which allows them to get comfortable, allows them to get a lot more efficient."
This is a win-win, he explained, as it's safer for the employees and there's less damage on the equipment due to inexperience.
Amanda Jacobs is a second-generation excavator operator who now trains new employees.
"I always liked equipment," she said. "Dad actually worked with Abitibi [paper company] in here, building roads and stuff. He was on an excavator and that got me interested in it, I guess."
A conveyor belt carries the crushed ore into the milling plant at the Valentine gold mine. (Leigh Anne Power/CBC)
And while workers on site make good, dependable salaries, they're not the only ones who benefit from Valentine, Cyr says.
He highlighted the use of local contractors and suppliers for the company's needs — from catering to T-shirts.
"So yeah, there's a lot of spinoff from this little asset we're sitting on here today," he said.
